{{legend0|#D3D3D3|No election}} }} '''United States gubernatorial elections''' were held in three states in 2015 as part of the [[United States elections, 2015|2015 United States elections]]. In [[Kentucky]] and [[Mississippi]], the elections were held on November 3, and in [[Louisiana]], as no candidate received a majority of votes at the primary election on October 24, 2015, a runoff election was held on November 21. The last regular gubernatorial elections for all three states were in [[2011 United States gubernatorial elections|2011]]. Democrats picked up the open seat of term-limited Republican [[Bobby Jindal]] in [[2015 Louisiana gubernatorial election|Louisiana]], while Republicans re-elected incumbent [[Phil Bryant]] in [[2015 Mississippi gubernatorial election|Mississippi]] and picked up the seat of term-limited Democrat [[Steve Beshear]] in [[2015 Kentucky gubernatorial election|Kentucky]]. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time that Republicans won the governorship in [[Kentucky]]. ==Election predictions== Several sites and individuals publish predictions of competitive seats. These predictions look at factors such as the strength of the [[incumbent]] (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assign ratings to each state, with the rating indicating the predicted advantage that a party has in winning that seat. Most election predictors use: * "tossup": no advantage * "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean" * "lean": slight advantage * "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage * "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory {|class="wikitable sortable" |+ !State ![[Cook Partisan Voting Index|PVI]] ! Under Louisiana's [[jungle primary]] system, all candidates, regardless of party, appear on the same ballot. The primary was held on October 24, 2015, with Democrat [[John Bel Edwards]] at 40% of the vote and Republican [[David Vitter]] at 23%. As no candidate won a majority of the vote, a runoff election between Edwards and Vitter was held on November 21, 2015.{{cite news|last1=Deslatte|first1=Melinda|title=Republican David Vitter reaches Louisiana governor's runoff against Democrat John Bel Edwards|url=https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2015/10/24/democrat-john-bel-edwards-heads-to-louisiana-governor-runoff|access-date=26 October 2015|agency=AP|publisher=U.S. News & World Report|date=25 October 2015}} Edwards won the runoff election with 56.1% of the vote, becoming the first Democrat to win a statewide election in Louisiana since 2008. '''Conway''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933E5|80–90%}} }} {{ElectionsKY}} The '''2015 Kentucky gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2015.{{cite web|author=Richard Pérez-Peña |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/30/us/james-comer-concedes-to-matt-bevin-in-kentucky-republican-governor-primary.html |title=Matt Bevin Prevails as James Comer Concedes Kentucky Governor Primary - The New York Times |publisher=Nytimes.com |access-date=2019-11-06}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Steve Beshear]] was ineligible to run for a third term due to [[Term limits in the United States|term limits]].{{cite web|last=Haberkorn |first=Jennifer |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2013/08/kentucky-obamacare-096101 |title=Kentucky's embrace of Obamacare |publisher=Politico |date=2013-08-31 |access-date=2019-11-06}} [[Partisan primary|Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2015. Despite trailing in most pre-election polls, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee [[Matt Bevin]] defeated Democratic nominee [[Jack Conway (politician)|Jack Conway]] by a margin of 52.5% to 43.8% in the general election. Statewide turnout in this election was 30%. With a margin of 8.7%, this election was the closest race of the [[2015 United States gubernatorial elections|2015 gubernatorial election cycle]]. This was the first time since [[2003 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2003]] that a Republican was elected governor of Kentucky, and the most recent time that this has occurred. This is the only instance in history in which [[Knott County, Kentucky|Knott County]] has backed a Republican candidate for governor. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Bobby Jindal]] was not eligible to run for re-election to a third term because of [[Term limits in the United States|term limits]] established by the [[Louisiana Constitution]]. Under Louisiana's [[Louisiana primary|jungle primary]] system, all candidates appeared on the same ballot, regardless of party and voters may vote for any candidate regardless of their party affiliation. As no candidate received a majority of the vote during the primary election on October 24, 2015, a runoff election was held on November 21, 2015, between the top two candidates in the primary. Louisiana is the only state that has a jungle primary system ([[California]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]] have a similar [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|"top two primary"]] system). The runoff election featured Democrat [[John Bel Edwards]], Minority Leader of the [[Louisiana House of Representatives]], and Republican [[United States Senator|U.S. senator]] [[David Vitter]], as they were the top two vote getters in the primary. Lieutenant Governor [[Jay Dardenne]] and Public Service Commissioner [[Scott Angelle]], both Republicans, were eliminated in the jungle primary. In the November 21, 2015 runoff, Edwards defeated Vitter by a count of 56.11% to 43.89% and was sworn in on January 11, 2016.{{cite web|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/louisiana-governors-runoff_n_564f4586e4b0879a5b0aa502|title=John Bel Edwards Wins Louisiana Gubernatorial Election|agency=ASSOCIATED PRESS|date=November 22, 2015|archive-date=November 22, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151122051747/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/entry/louisiana-governors-runoff_564f4586e4b0879a5b0aa502|url-status=live|work=The Huffington Post}}{{Cite web |title=John Bel Edwards |url=https://www.nga.org/governor/john-bel-edwards/ |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=National Governors Association}} This was the only statewide victory in 2015 for Democrats in Louisiana, and was the first time Democrats won a statewide election in the state since [[Mary Landrieu]] won her third term in the [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] in [[2008 United States Senate election in Louisiana|2008]]. Edwards' victory also came one year after [[2014 United States elections|national wins for the Republican Party]] in congressional and state elections, including Landrieu’s failed 2014 re-election bid. This was the first election since [[1968 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1968]] that a Democratic candidate for governor won during a Democratic presidency. The election was one of the most expensive in state history, with over $50 million spent by the candidates and outside groups.{{cite web |title=$50M spent on Louisiana governor race, campaign records show |url=http://www.thenewsstar.com/story/news/local/2016/01/09/spent-louisiana-governor-race-campaign-records-show/78568696/ |website=thenewsstar.com |access-date=January 22, 2016}} ==Candidates== ===Republican Party=== ====Filed==== * [[Scott Angelle]], [[Louisiana Public Service Commission|Public Service Commissioner]] and former [[lieutenant governor of Louisiana]]{{cite web|url=http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2014/10/scott_angelle_to_run_for_gover.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141005002434/http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2014/10/scott_angelle_to_run_for_gover.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 5, 2014|title=Scott Angelle to run for governor in 2015|date=October 2, 2014|access-date=October 2, 2014|work=[[The Times-Picayune]]|first=Cole|last=Avery}} * [[Jay Dardenne]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Louisiana]]{{cite web|url=http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2013/03/lt_gov_jay_dardenne_intends_to.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130616061939/http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2013/03/lt_gov_jay_dardenne_intends_to.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 16, 2013|title=Lt. [[2008 United States Senate election in Louisiana|2008]]. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} | flag_year = 2001 }} {{ElectionsMS}} The '''2015 Mississippi gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2015, to elect the [[List of Governors of Mississippi|governor of Mississippi]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Phil Bryant]] won a second and final term in office with more than 66% of votes, the highest percentage and vote share that a Republican has ever won in a gubernatorial election in Mississippi. The election gained national news coverage and attention due to the unexpected Democratic nominee selection of truck driver and former firefighter, Robert Gray, who had not had any political experience prior to his candidacy.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/08/us/shy-trucker-emerges-as-democrats-pick-for-mississippi-governor.html|title=Chosen by Mississippi Democrats, Shy Trucker is at a Crossroad|newspaper=The New York Times|date=7 September 2015|last1=Robertson|first1=Campbell}} As of 2026, this is the last time that the following counties have voted Republican for governor: [[Clay County, Mississippi|Clay]], [[Marshall County, Mississippi|Marshall]], [[Quitman County, Mississippi|Quitman]], [[Sharkey County, Mississippi|Sharkey]], and [[Tallahatchie County, Mississippi|Tallahatchie]]. ==Background== Mississippi is one of nine states and territories that has lifetime limits of two terms for its governor. In [[Mississippi gubernatorial election, 2011|2011]], with incumbent Republican governor [[Haley Barbour]] term-limited, Republican [[Lieutenant Governor of Mississippi|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Phil Bryant]] was elected to succeed him. Bryant won the Republican primary with 59% of the vote and then defeated the Democratic nominee, [[Hattiesburg, Mississippi|Hattiesburg]] Mayor [[Johnny DuPree]], with 61% of the vote. ==Republican
